hints: Focus on the conditions, not just the reagents. Aqueous and ethanolic NaOH do very different jobs with a haloalkane.
Remember that $\text{OH}^-$ in ethanol acts mainly as a base, removing a $\text{H}^+$ from the carbon next to the $\text{C-Br}$ carbon.
Think about what forms when $\text{HBr}$ is effectively removed from $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Br}$, and what reaction type makes an alkene from a haloalkane.
walkthrough:
**Recall the two jobs of hydroxide**

Hydroxide can act as a nucleophile to replace Br, or as a base to remove H. Which job it does depends on the solvent.

$$\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Br} + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{substitution OR elimination}$$

**Read the condition: NaOH in ethanol**

Aqueous NaOH (water) gives nucleophilic substitution to an alcohol. Ethanolic NaOH (ethanol) heated gives elimination to an alkene. Here we have ethanol, so think base.

$$\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Br} + \text{NaOH (ethanolic, heat)} \rightarrow \text{CH}_2=\text{CH}_2 + \text{NaBr} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Confirm the product type**

Removing H from one carbon and Br from the adjacent carbon forms a C=C double bond. That loss of a small molecule to form an unsaturated product is dehydrohalogenation, a classic elimination.

options.A: Electrophilic substitution happens with benzene rings and electrophiles, not with haloalkanes and $\text{OH}^-$. Here $\text{OH}^-$ is a nucleophile or base attacking an electron-deficient carbon, so this type is incorrect.
options.B: Heating with ethanolic NaOH makes $\text{OH}^-$ act as a base. It removes a hydrogen from the beta-carbon while bromide leaves, giving ethene. This is elimination (dehydrohalogenation).
options.C: Two problems here. Ethanolic conditions favour elimination, not substitution. Also, bromoethane is primary and would not react mainly by SN1, which needs a stable tertiary carbocation.
options.D: This is the classic trap. Aqueous NaOH with primary bromoethane would indeed give nucleophilic substitution via SN2, but the question uses NaOH in ethanol with heat, which switches the pathway to elimination.
